common_name: Golden Torch Cardinal Flower (Yellow-Leaved Cardinal Flower)

planting.note: Plant divisions or potted starts in spring into consistently moist, humus-rich soil near a pond edge, rain garden, or low wet spot; give 'Golden Torch' a half-day of direct sun rather than deep shade, since bright light intensifies the gold foliage color and plants grown too dark tend to green out.

directions: Golden Torch is the first cardinal flower selected for bright gold-yellow foliage rather than green or burgundy, a seedling sport originated by Brent Horvath of Intrinsic Perennial Gardens in Illinois and later also produced and sold through Terra Nova Nurseries. The glowing foliage holds its color from spring into summer and sets off the two-lipped scarlet flower spikes that rise above it from midsummer into fall, drawing ruby-throated hummingbirds just as the species does. Because it is propagated only by division and tissue culture rather than seed, plants come true to the gold leaf color year after year instead of reverting the way seedling-grown colored forms often do. Keep soil consistently moist to wet and give a few hours of direct sun daily; deep, constant shade dulls the foliage toward plain green.
sources: US Plant Patent PP19,844 (Google Patents, inventor Brent Horvath, Intrinsic Perennial Gardens)

planting.note: Divide rhizome sections in early spring and plant in consistently moist, rich soil in bright to open shade; confine with a buried barrier or a naturally wet, bounded site, since variegated butterbur spreads by rhizomes almost as readily as the plain green species.

directions: Also sold under its Japanese name Nishiki-buki, this form of Japanese butterbur carries bold rounded leaves irregularly marbled and streaked with creamy white to pale yellow, the variegation brightest on young spring growth before fading toward green as summer heat sets in. It is noticeably smaller and less overwhelming than the plain-leaved 'Giganteus' form, making it a more manageable choice for a bold accent at the edge of a shaded, boggy bed or pond margin. Clusters of small, pale, fragrant flowers appear on stout scapes very early in spring, well before the leaves unfurl. A little open sky or morning sun helps keep the pale variegation crisp, while deep, dry shade both dulls the pattern and weakens the plant.

common_name: Little Lantern Ligularia (Compact Hybrid Leopard Plant)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into consistently moist, humus-rich, fertile soil in partial shade; 'Little Lantern' stays far more compact than 'The Rocket' or even 'Bottle Rocket', so it fits in smaller borders, large containers, and pond-edge plantings where bigger ligularias would overwhelm the space.

directions: A German-raised hybrid also sold as 'Laternchen', Little Lantern forms a dense, tidy clump of broad, toothed, dark green leaves topped from mid- to late summer by conical spikes of small, brilliant yellow daisy flowers packed tightly along the stem rather than the loose spires typical of Ligularia stenocephala selections. Its small stature relative to most ligularias makes it useful where the dramatic bold foliage of this shade-loving genus is wanted without the two-to-four-foot bulk of 'Desdemona' or 'The Rocket'. Like all ligularias it wilts visibly in dry soil or hot afternoon sun, so keep it in cool, consistently moist to wet ground in shade or morning sun only. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor and flowering.
